main.title: Street Fighter III
main.summary: Street Fighter III: New Generation is a 1997 fighting game in Capcom's Street Fighter series, originally released as a coin-operated arcade game.

cards.heading: A new generation of fighters
cards.text: Street Fighter III: New Generation is a 1997 fighting game in Capcom's Street Fighter series, originally released as a coin-operated arcade game. The sequel to Street Fighter II (1991), it initially discarded every previous character except for Ryu and Ken (hence the New Generation subtitle), introducing an all-new roster led by Alex. Likewise, a new antagonist named Gill took over M. Bison's role from the previous games as the new boss character.

cards.heading: CP System III keeps the fight in 2D
cards.text: Street Fighter III was produced for the CD-ROM-based CP System III hardware, which allowed for more elaborate 2D graphics than the CPS II-based Street Fighter Alpha games (the previous incarnation of the Street Fighter series), while revamping many of the play mechanics. Despite the popularity of 3D polygonal fighting games at the time, Capcom decided to keep this game in 2D; 3D graphics were instead implemented in the spin-off game, Street Fighter EX.

cards.heading: Second Impact, Third Strike and the home editions
cards.text: Street Fighter III was followed by two updates: 2nd Impact in 1997, and 3rd Strike in 1999. A single home version of the game was released for the Dreamcast in 1999 and 2000, in a two-in-one compilation titled Street Fighter III: Double Impact, which consists of New Generation and 2nd Impact. Street Fighter III received a mainly positive reception, but did not manage to be a hit like its predecessor; it was followed by Street Fighter IV (2008).

main.title: Bushido Blade
main.subtitle: A duel decided by one opening
main.summary: Bushido Blade is Lightweight's 1997 PlayStation fighting game about armed duels, first released in Japan on 14 March. A sword strike can end the encounter immediately, making a small error more important than a long sequence of successful attacks. Six fighters and eight weapons offer different combinations of speed, reach and strength. The absence of a health bar changes the rhythm of watching an opponent: every approach could become the final exchange. Waiting, retreating and choosing a stance become as meaningful as the moment a weapon finally moves.

cards.heading: A duel decided by one opening
cards.text: Bushido Blade is Lightweight's 1997 PlayStation fighting game about armed duels, first released in Japan on 14 March. A sword strike can end the encounter immediately, making a small error more important than a long sequence of successful attacks. Six fighters and eight weapons offer different combinations of speed, reach and strength. The absence of a health bar changes the rhythm of watching an opponent: every approach could become the final exchange. Waiting, retreating and choosing a stance become as meaningful as the moment a weapon finally moves.

cards.heading: An injury changes the fight
cards.text: A blow can wound without killing. Damage to an arm may remove two-handed attacks or the ability to throw a secondary weapon; injured legs can leave a fighter crawling. The Body Damage System therefore changes the actions available during the duel instead of simply subtracting a number. High, neutral and low stances provide different attacks, while the Motion Shift System connects one swing to another. A successful defence preserves more than life: it keeps movement and weapons available for the next attempt to find a vulnerable angle.

cards.heading: Room to step away
cards.text: The fighters can run, jump and climb through connected parts of a castle compound, including a grove, moat and maze of bridges. Combat can move beyond the small space where it began. A katana, rapier or naginata makes distance useful in a different way, so choosing where to stand is part of choosing how to fight. Bushido Blade attracted attention for this unusual treatment of damage and freedom of movement. A direct sequel followed on PlayStation in 1998, continuing an alternative to the round-based exchanges familiar from contemporary fighting games.

main.title: Castlevania: Symphony of the Night
main.summary: Castlevania: Symphony of the Night is a 1997 action role-playing game developed and published by Konami for the PlayStation and Sega Saturn.

cards.heading: A sequel to Rondo of Blood
cards.text: Castlevania: Symphony of the Night is a 1997 action role-playing game developed and published by Konami for the PlayStation and Sega Saturn. It is a direct sequel to Castlevania: Rondo of Blood, set five years after its events. It was directed and produced by Toru Hagihara, with Koji Igarashi acting as assistant director.

cards.heading: Exploration changes the structure of Castlevania
cards.text: It features Dracula's dhampir son Alucard (returning from Castlevania III: Dracula's Curse) as the protagonist, as he explores Dracula's castle (which reemerges following the disappearance of Richter Belmont) and fights to prevent his father from fully regaining his lost power. Its design marks a break from previous entries in the series, re-introducing the exploration, nonlinear level design, and role-playing elements first experimented with in Castlevania II: Simon's Quest.

cards.heading: Word of mouth and a lasting design influence
cards.text: Symphony of the Night initially sold poorly. However, it gradually gained sales through word-of-mouth and became a sleeper hit, developing a cult following and selling over 700,000 units in the United States and Japan. The game garnered acclaim, often cited by critics as one of the best video games of all time, praising its gameplay innovations, atmosphere, visuals and soundtrack with criticism directed towards the voice acting. It is also considered the definitive pioneer of the Metroidvania genre, combining the two games and inspiring numerous exploration-based action-adventure games ever since. Symphony of the Night would have a lasting impact on the Castlevania series, with numerous subsequent mainline entries adopting its gameplay model.

main.title: Blast Corps
main.subtitle: Rare · Nintendo 64
main.summary: Blast Corps is Rare's Nintendo 64 action-puzzle game about clearing a route for a runaway nuclear missile carrier. Buildings and other obstacles must be removed before the vehicle reaches them, using a collection of demolition machines found around each location. The premise makes destruction an urgent practical task. A large building is a problem because it occupies the wrong place, and the player has to discover which machine can remove it quickly enough while the carrier continues moving towards it.

cards.heading: Clear the road before the carrier arrives
cards.text: Blast Corps is Rare's Nintendo 64 action-puzzle game about clearing a route for a runaway nuclear missile carrier. Buildings and other obstacles must be removed before the vehicle reaches them, using a collection of demolition machines found around each location. The premise makes destruction an urgent practical task. A large building is a problem because it occupies the wrong place, and the player has to discover which machine can remove it quickly enough while the carrier continues moving towards it.

cards.heading: Every machine destroys differently
cards.text: The bulldozer can ram structures, while other vehicles rely on sliding, dropping from a height or a robot's particular movement. Changing machines is essential when a route presents more than one kind of obstruction. Crates of explosives and other machinery add problems that require preparation before the last building can fall. The player studies the location as a sequence of jobs, deciding what should be moved or destroyed first and which useful vehicle needs to be waiting nearby when that task is complete.

cards.heading: Return when the emergency is over
cards.text: After securing the carrier's route, the player can revisit a location to destroy remaining structures, activate lights and find secrets without the same immediate pressure. Medal targets and further challenges then turn that knowledge into faster, more accurate attempts. Developed by a small Rare team and released in 1997, Blast Corps found another use for the new console's three-dimensional worlds. The scenery becomes a working problem whose solution is visible in the empty space left behind when the appropriate machine has done its job.

main.title: Theme Hospital
main.summary: Theme Hospital is a business simulation game developed by Bullfrog Productions and published by Electronic Arts in 1997 for MS-DOS and Microsoft Windows compatible PCs in which players design and operate a privately owned hospital with the goal of curing patients of fictitious comical ailments.

cards.heading: Theme Hospital
cards.text: Theme Hospital is a business simulation game developed by Bullfrog Productions and published by Electronic Arts in 1997 for MS-DOS and Microsoft Windows compatible PCs in which players design and operate a privately owned hospital with the goal of curing patients of fictitious comical ailments. The game is the thematic successor to Theme Park, also produced by Bullfrog, and the second installment in their Theme series, and part of their Designer Series. The game is noted for its humour, and contains numerous references to pop culture.

cards.heading: Hospital humour under production deadlines
cards.text: Peter Molyneux and James Leach came up with the idea of creating a Theme game based on a hospital, but Molyneux was not directly involved in development due to his work on Dungeon Keeper. Designers originally planned to include four distinct gameplay modes corresponding to historical time periods, but this was dropped due to time pressures on the team. Multiplayer support with up to four players was added in a patch. The game received a generally positive reception, with reviewers praising the graphics and humour in particular. Theme Hospital was a commercial success, selling over 4 million copies worldwide, and was ported to the PlayStation in 1998. A Saturn version was in development, but cancelled. The game was re-released on GOG.com in 2012 and Origin in 2014, and the PlayStation version was released on the PlayStation Network in Europe in 2008, Japan in 2009, and North America in 2010. Revival attempts have been made with the development of open-source remakes such as CorsixTH.

main.title: Alundra
main.subtitle: The village behind the nightmares
main.summary: Alundra is Matrix Software's PlayStation action-adventure, first released in Japan on 11 April 1997. A young dreamwalker survives a shipwreck and reaches Inoa, a village whose people suffer recurring nightmares. His ability to enter those dreams gives him a way to help, but deaths and suspicion gradually make the refuge less welcoming. The island and its dungeons combine exploration, real-time combat and demanding puzzles. The setting gives those familiar activities a personal connection: the next strange place may exist inside someone met earlier in the village.

cards.heading: The village behind the nightmares
cards.text: Alundra is Matrix Software's PlayStation action-adventure, first released in Japan on 11 April 1997. A young dreamwalker survives a shipwreck and reaches Inoa, a village whose people suffer recurring nightmares. His ability to enter those dreams gives him a way to help, but deaths and suspicion gradually make the refuge less welcoming. The island and its dungeons combine exploration, real-time combat and demanding puzzles. The setting gives those familiar activities a personal connection: the next strange place may exist inside someone met earlier in the village.

cards.heading: A dream becomes a dungeon
cards.text: Each dream reflects the person experiencing it, allowing the adventure to change its surroundings without leaving the villagers behind. Outside those sequences, Alundra searches an island of terrain and obstacles that react differently to his movement. Sand slows him and lava causes damage; later improvements can make previously difficult routes manageable. Fighting and platforming require attention to position, while puzzles ask him to understand how the space fits together. Returning to Inoa connects these excursions to people whose condition gives the next journey a reason beyond finding another treasure.

cards.heading: Coming home to a darker story
cards.text: Jess shelters Alundra after the wreck, establishing a home from which the player repeatedly leaves and returns. As the nightmares continue, some villagers blame the newcomer for the tragedies around them. That changing reception makes a familiar place feel less secure. The story addresses death, faith and despair through its small community, with Kōhei Tanaka's music accompanying the contrast between refuge and danger. The North American release followed in 1997, with Europe receiving the game in 1998, and critics praised the characterisation and challenging puzzles. Alundra 2 appeared in 1999 as a separate adventure rather than a continuation of this village's story.

main.title: Tobal 2
main.subtitle: A larger world behind the fighting arena
main.summary: Tobal 2 is DreamFactory's PlayStation fighting game, released in Japan on 25 April 1997. It expands the original's combination of three-dimensional duels and dungeon exploration, retaining characters designed by Akira Toriyama. Fighters move around one another while keeping their attention on the opponent, using high, middle and low attacks alongside grappling and defence. The sequel adds more possibilities without abandoning that physical relationship. Its greatly enlarged Quest mode makes the arena part of a wider activity, encouraging the player to explore and build a collection as well as win the next conventional match.

cards.heading: A larger world behind the fighting arena
cards.text: Tobal 2 is DreamFactory's PlayStation fighting game, released in Japan on 25 April 1997. It expands the original's combination of three-dimensional duels and dungeon exploration, retaining characters designed by Akira Toriyama. Fighters move around one another while keeping their attention on the opponent, using high, middle and low attacks alongside grappling and defence. The sequel adds more possibilities without abandoning that physical relationship. Its greatly enlarged Quest mode makes the arena part of a wider activity, encouraging the player to explore and build a collection as well as win the next conventional match.

cards.heading: Bring another opponent into the collection
cards.text: Quest mode gives the fighting system a longer structure, with a large roster available through progress and discoveries. The expanded cast offers many different bodies through which to learn the same underlying rules. A new fireball attack gives each character another option, while movement and close grappling remain important. The player still has to decide when to advance, circle or hold a defensive position. The size of the collection becomes meaningful because another unlocked fighter can change the practical feel of confronting a familiar opponent, rather than serving only as another name on a selection screen.

cards.heading: A sequel that stayed in Japan
cards.text: Seiichi Ishii returned as director, with Takayuki Nakamura composing the music. The game improved its character shading and resolution while retaining smooth sixty-frame-per-second action. It launched alongside Sony's Dual Analog Controller in Japan and supported the new peripheral. Unlike Tobal No. 1, it was not released internationally. Its two hundred playable characters later gave it a record-setting reputation, but its distinctive appeal also lies in the expanded Quest mode: the fighting game becomes something to inhabit over time, with discoveries continuing beyond the next tournament victory.

main.title: Star Fox 64
main.subtitle: One squadron, many routes
main.summary: Released in Japan on April 27, 1997, Star Fox 64 brought Nintendo’s space-shooting squadron to Nintendo 64. Europe knew the same game as Lylat Wars. Fox pilots the Arwing, Landmaster tank and Blue Marine submarine through a campaign whose route changes with the player’s actions. Hidden objectives make a successful mission more than a question of reaching its end: another attempt can reveal a different planet, encounter or approach to Venom.

cards.heading: A route earned in flight
cards.text: Released in Japan on April 27, 1997, Star Fox 64 brought Nintendo’s space-shooting squadron to Nintendo 64. Europe knew the same game as Lylat Wars. Fox pilots the Arwing, Landmaster tank and Blue Marine submarine through a campaign whose route changes with the player’s actions. Hidden objectives make a successful mission more than a question of reaching its end: another attempt can reveal a different planet, encounter or approach to Venom.

cards.heading: A conversation inside the battle
cards.text: The wingmen turn that route into a shared journey. Their radio calls interrupt the shooting with warnings, requests and arguments; protecting them is part of managing the battle. Forward-scrolling stages alternate with freely manoeuvrable All-Range encounters, and a separate versus mode supports up to four players.

main.title: Atelier Marie: The Alchemist of Salburg
main.subtitle: Five years to become an alchemist
main.summary: Gust released Atelier Marie for PlayStation in Japan on May 23, 1997.

cards.heading: An atelier in Salburg
cards.text: Gust released Atelier Marie for PlayStation in Japan on May 23, 1997. Marlone is a struggling academy student who receives an atelier and a chance to prove her ability. Gathering ingredients, learning recipes and synthesising items shape her work. Time, commissions and the results of her experiments give this role-playing adventure its daily routine.

cards.heading: Planning a five-year examination
cards.text: Marlone has five years to create an item that demonstrates her ability as an alchemist. Travelling, gathering, making items and accepting jobs all consume days. Choosing one expedition can reduce the time available for another task, so the calendar gives even quiet activities a practical cost. Planning the atelier's work becomes part of advancing through the game.

cards.heading: Making items from materials
cards.text: Synthesis combines gathered materials with acquired knowledge to produce useful items. A plant, mineral or rare ingredient can be valuable because of a recipe it helps complete. Exploration supplies materials, while learning how they can be combined guides later expeditions. Making items is therefore a central form of progression throughout the adventure.

cards.heading: Learning through the work
cards.text: Marlone's difficulties at the academy give the story room for learning, friendships and mistakes. What the player achieves during the five years can lead to different outcomes. Her development is measured through acquired skills and completed work as she tries to establish herself as an alchemist.

main.title: The recording session behind an island
main.summary: A preserved ADR-session tape records part of Riven’s 1997 production.

cards.heading: A session recorded in May 1997
cards.text: The Video Game History Foundation catalogue identifies a Riven ADR recording session dated May 29, 1997. Its Betacam SP tape carries the working label Myst II Audio Session. The date locates this recording work within the game's production. Scheduled sessions and recorded performances were among the materials used to build the island players would later encounter.

cards.heading: Camera footage and composite tests
cards.text: The wider Cyan collection includes raw camera footage, composite tests, developer interviews and behind-the-scenes material from Riven. Together these records preserve stages between a performance in front of a camera and its appearance inside the finished game. Composite tests show how filmed material was being combined with the surrounding scenes.

cards.heading: Related recordings in the archive
cards.text: The item description notes that its footage overlaps another ADR-session video in the collection. The two catalogue records therefore preserve related material from the recording process. The entry establishes the session date and tape format, while identifying individual speakers and dialogue requires examining the footage itself.

cards.heading: Revisiting the island in 2024
cards.text: Cyan's 2024 reimagining of Riven added changed puzzles, expanded narrative and movement through the scenes. Project manager Ryan Warzecha described discussions involving members of the original team and consultation with Robyn Miller. The later project revisited the same world with new production methods, while the preserved 1997 materials document how its first version was made.
